title: Round 1 — if/else logic, nothing they can recite (Python or JavaScript)

round1.title: Alarm Clock
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take the current hour and the hour the alarm is set for. Both are 0 to 23.

• Print how many hours until the alarm rings.
• If the alarm hour is the same as now, it rings in 24 hours.

Examples:

9  14   → 5
22  3   → 5
23  0   → 1
0  23   → 23
9  9    → 24

The second example is the one to think about. It is 10pm and the alarm is set for 3am.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if alarm > now:
    print(alarm - now)
else:
    if alarm < now: print(24 - now + alarm)
    else:           print(24)

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces. Convert both inputs with Number() — if
they are still strings, alarm - now works (minus coerces) but alarm > now
compares character by character, so "9" > "14" is TRUE and the whole thing
inverts.

TESTING: arithmetic that wraps around. Midnight is not a special case to be
patched afterwards — it is the whole question.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 22 3 prints -19. They wrote alarm - now and stopped. THIS IS THE TRAP and it is
  the most common answer. Test 22 3 before anything else.
- 22 3 prints 19. They noticed the negative and used abs(), which is not the same
  thing — check 23 0 as well, which should be 1 and abs() gives 23.
- 9 9 prints 0. An alarm set for the current hour rings tomorrow.
- 23 0 prints 23 or -23.

CHECK: 22 3, then 23 0, then 9 9.

round1.title: Battery Message
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take the battery percentage, and whether the phone is plugged in ("yes" or "no").

Print one message:

• Plugged in and at 100 → "Fully charged"
• Plugged in → "Charging"
• 5 or below → "Plug in now"
• 20 or below → "Low battery"
• Anything else → "Battery fine"

Examples:

100 yes  → Fully charged
45 yes   → Charging
3 yes    → Charging
3 no     → Plug in now
15 no    → Low battery
80 no    → Battery fine
100 no   → Battery fine

Read the third example. The phone is nearly flat, but it is plugged in.

round1.title: Wi-Fi Bars
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Take the Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm. It is always a NEGATIVE number, and
closer to zero means a stronger signal.

• -50 or stronger → "4 bars"
• -60 or stronger → "3 bars"
• -70 or stronger → "2 bars"
• -80 or stronger → "1 bar"
• Weaker than -80 → "No signal"

Examples:

-45   → 4 bars
-50   → 4 bars
-55   → 3 bars
-70   → 2 bars
-80   → 1 bar
-85   → No signal

-45 is a STRONGER signal than -85. Get that straight before you write anything.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if signal >= -50:   print("4 bars")
elif signal >= -60: print("3 bars")
elif signal >= -70: print("2 bars")
elif signal >= -80: print("1 bar")
else:               print("No signal")

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces. Convert with Number() — a minus sign in a
string is where coercion gets strange, and "-45" >= -50 is not something to rely
on by accident.

TESTING: whether they can hold a reversed scale in their head. Every threshold
question they have ever done went the other way, so the instinct to write <=
is strong and completely wrong here.

MARK WRONG IF:
- -45 prints "No signal" or falls through to the bottom. They wrote <= because
  "smaller number is worse" — but -45 is not smaller than -50. THIS IS THE TRAP,
  and it is most of the wrong answers. Test -45 first.
- -85 prints "1 bar". They forgot the final else.
- -50 prints "3 bars" — the boundary; "-50 or stronger" includes -50.
- They wrote the bands in the wrong order, so -45 matches -80 first and prints
  "1 bar".

CHECK: -45, then -85, then -50.

round1.title: Snakes and Ladders
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

You are on a square between 1 and 99. Take your square, your dice roll (1 to 6),
then one special square and where it leads.

• If the roll would take you past 100, you do not move → print "Stay"
• If it lands you exactly on 100 → print "Won"
• If it lands you on the special square → print where that leads
• Otherwise → print your new square

Examples:

94  6   30 12   → Won
97  5   30 12   → Stay
20  5   25 60   → 60
20  3   25 60   → 23
50  4   54 12   → 12

The special square can be a ladder up or a snake down. It does not matter which.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
next_sq = square + roll

if next_sq > 100:
    print("Stay")
else:
    if next_sq == 100:
        print("Won")
    else:
        if next_sq == special: print(destination)
        else:                  print(next_sq)

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces. Convert everything with Number() FIRST —
square + roll on strings gives "20" + "5" = "205", which is greater than 100 and
silently prints "Stay" for every single roll.

TESTING: three special cases that all have to be checked before the ordinary one,
in the right order. Working out the new square once at the top, then asking
questions about it, is the shape that makes this easy — recomputing square + roll
inside every branch is where the mistakes come from.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 94 6 30 12 prints 100 instead of "Won". They handled the overshoot but not the
  exact landing. THE TRAP.
- 97 5 30 12 prints 102. No overshoot check at all.
- 20 5 25 60 prints 25. They checked the special square after printing, or never.
- They check the special square BEFORE the win, which is only wrong if 100 is
  also a special square — mention it, do not deduct.

CHECK: 94 6 30 12, then 97 5 30 12, then 20 5 25 60.

round1.title: Wordle Tile
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

One tile of a Wordle guess. Take three things:

• the letter you guessed
• the letter the secret word actually has in that position
• whether your letter appears somewhere else in the secret word ("yes" or "no")

Print the colour of the tile:

• Right letter, right position → "Green"
• Wrong position, but the letter is in the word → "Yellow"
• Not in the word at all → "Grey"

Examples:

a  a  no    → Green
e  e  yes   → Green
a  b  yes   → Yellow
a  b  no    → Grey
s  t  yes   → Yellow

Look at the second example carefully.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if guess == actual:
    print("Green")
else:
    if elsewhere == "yes": print("Yellow")
    else:                  print("Grey")

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces, comparing with === . No Number()
conversion needed here — these are letters, and this is the one question in the
set where strings are what you actually want.

TESTING: precedence again, but subtler than it looks. A letter can be in the
right position AND appear elsewhere in the word at the same time — "e e yes" is
exactly that — and green has to win.

MARK WRONG IF:
- e e yes prints "Yellow". They checked "appears elsewhere" before checking the
  position. THIS IS THE TRAP, and the example is in the question precisely so a
  careful student catches it.
- a a no prints "Grey". They required "elsewhere" to be yes before considering
  green at all.
- Three separate ifs with no else, printing two colours for one tile.

CHECK: e e yes, then a a no, then a b no.

round1.title: Which Lift Comes
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

A building has two lifts. Take the floor Lift 1 is on, the floor Lift 2 is on,
and the floor you are standing on.

• Print "Lift 1" or "Lift 2" — whichever is fewer floors away.
• If they are the same distance away, print "Either".

Examples:

3  9  5   → Lift 1
3  9  8   → Lift 2
2  8  5   → Either
5  5  1   → Either
0  4  4   → Lift 2

RULE: you may NOT use abs(). Work out each distance yourself.

A lift can be above you or below you, and you do not know which.
round1.answerKey:
REFERENCE (Python):
if lift1 > me: d1 = lift1 - me
else:          d1 = me - lift1

if lift2 > me: d2 = lift2 - me
else:          d2 = me - lift2

if d1 < d2: print("Lift 1")
else:
    if d2 < d1: print("Lift 2")
    else:       print("Either")

IN JAVASCRIPT: same shape with braces. Convert all three with Number() — the
subtractions coerce and work, but the > comparisons compare as text, so a lift on
floor 9 looks further than one on floor 10.

TESTING: building a distance without the function that does it for you, and
noticing that "fewer floors away" needs THREE outcomes, not two.

MARK WRONG IF:
- 3 9 8 prints "Lift 1". They wrote lift1 - me without handling the lift being
  below them, so a negative distance looked smaller. THIS IS THE TRAP — the buggy
  code happens to give the right answer on 3 9 5, so test 3 9 8 first or you will
  pass code that is broken.
- 2 8 5 prints "Lift 1" or "Lift 2". No "Either" branch — an if/else with two
  outcomes cannot express a tie.
- They used abs() anyway. The logic is right; the exercise was the two-branch
  distance. Your call on partial credit.

CHECK: 3 9 8, then 2 8 5, then 0 4 4.

round1.title: Dice Duel
round1.prompt:
Write it in Python or JavaScript — your choice.

Two players roll two dice each. Take Player 1's two dice, then Player 2's two dice.

• A double (both dice the same) beats any non-double, whatever the totals.
• If BOTH roll doubles, the higher double wins.
• If neither rolls a double, the higher total wins.
• Still level → "Draw".

Examples:

2 2   6 5   → Player 1
6 5   2 2   → Player 2
3 3   5 5   → Player 2
4 4   4 4   → Draw
6 3   5 4   → Draw
6 4   5 3   → Player 1

In the first example Player 1 scores 4 and Player 2 scores 11 — and Player 1 wins.
